articles.title: Moishe Mana spent 16 years assembling about 30 acres in Miami’s Wynwood district; Ken Griffin has now bought the land for about $1.1 billion in Florida’s largest land-assemblage deal, with a university campus planned
articles.summary: Moishe Mana began buying property in Miami’s Wynwood district in 2009, when the area was still largely abandoned and in the early stages of transformation.
articles.body: Moishe Mana began buying property in Miami’s Wynwood district in 2009, when the area was still largely abandoned and in the early stages of transformation. Over 16 years, he assembled roughly 30 acres into what became Mana Wynwood, a cultural and events hub known for art fairs, concerts and festivals. On September 29, 2026, Mana Common closed the sale of that assemblage to Citadel founder and CEO Ken Griffin for approximately $1.1 billion, a transaction the company describes as the largest land-assemblage deal in Florida history, as per Hauteresidence.com. The site is planned to become part of a new Carnegie Mellon University campus in Wynwood.From distressed warehouse to cultural hubMana’s first major purchase in Wynwood was a distressed warehouse acquired for about $5 million, which became the foundation of Mana Wynwood. Over the years, he invested less than $70 million to assemble his holdings in the area, according to Mana Common. The property evolved into one of the district’s largest cultural venues, hosting events such as Miami Music Week and the III Points festival.Mana’s approach drew on his earlier experience in New York City’s Meatpacking District, where he established Milk Studios during that neighbourhood’s early redevelopment. He applied a similar model in Wynwood, investing not only in real estate but also in street art, music, fashion and community programming. Mana Common says it spent roughly $2 million to $3 million annually on neighbourhood culture, helping shape Wynwood’s identity as a creative district, as per reports.That investment strategy reflected a belief that culture and commerce could grow together. By creating a space that attracted artists, musicians, designers and event organisers, Mana helped establish Wynwood as a destination. The sale to Griffin marks a new phase, with the focus shifting from cultural programming to education and technology.The scale of the Griffin purchaseThe approximately $1.1 billion price works out to about $36.7 million per acre, or roughly $842 per square foot of land, based on 30 acres equalling 1,306,800 square feet. Mana Common describes the deal as the largest land-assemblage transaction in Florida’s history, reflecting both the size of the holding and the strategic value of the location. The sale includes the Mana Wynwood campus at 318 NW 23rd Street, which has operated as a cultural and events venue. Ken Griffin is the founder and CEO of Citadel and the founder of Griffin Catalyst. His purchase of the Wynwood land is part of a broader commitment to Miami, where he has been building a significant presence. The transaction links that financial presence to a planned research and workforce platform centred on Carnegie Mellon University.For Mana, the sale represents a return on a long-term bet. Using only the disclosed figures, the sale price represents a gross value uplift of at least approximately $1.03 billion, or more than 15 times the stated investment, before accounting for operating, cultural, carrying, financing, entitlement and transaction costs, the report suggests. These are indicative calculations rather than realised profit figures, but they illustrate the scale of the appreciation.Carnegie Mellon’s planned Wynwood campusCarnegie Mellon University announced a $3 billion gift from Griffin, which the university describes as the largest individual philanthropic investment in higher education. Of that amount, $2 billion is earmarked for the Miami campus and $1 billion for Carnegie Mellon’s Pittsburgh campus and broader academic priorities. The Miami campus is planned to occupy more than 35 acres in Wynwood, indicating that the university’s footprint may include land beyond the parcels sold by Mana Common, reported Haute Residence.At full scale, the campus is planned to support more than 3,500 undergraduate, master’s and doctoral students, with nearly 300 faculty members and more than 600 staff. Construction is expected to begin in 2027, with graduate enrolment targeted for 2028 and undergraduate enrolment expected four years later, subject to regulatory approvals. The campus will include industry research labs and venture studios, positioning it as a hub for innovation alongside education, it further reported.Planned areas of focus include human health, biodiversity, national security, energy and climate resilience, advanced manufacturing and industrial transformation. These fields align with the broader vision of Wynwood as a place where technology, education and industry converge. Carnegie Mellon President Farnam Jahanian has described the Miami campus as a sister or peer campus rather than a satellite, underscoring its importance to the university’s future.What the sale means for WynwoodThe transaction reflects a shift in Wynwood from its initial creative and cultural redevelopment phase toward an education- and technology-oriented land use. Carnegie Mellon’s planned presence could generate demand for housing, research space, retail, hospitality, student services and innovation-focused companies. The campus is expected to bring thousands of students, faculty and staff to the area over time.Student housing is part of the plan, with dormitories mentioned by Jahanian in comments to the Miami Herald. The number of beds and their exact location have not been disclosed, so it is not yet clear how much demand will reach the private rental and condo market. For nearby residents and property owners, the campus represents a long-term institutional anchor that could reshape the neighbourhood’s character.Mana Common retains more than 15 acres in the Wynwood area and says it will continue to invest in the neighbourhood. The company will also continue to oversee operations and maintain existing events at the Mana Wynwood space for the foreseeable future. That continuity suggests that the cultural programming that helped define the district will not disappear overnight.Mana’s broader Miami visionBeyond Wynwood, Moishe Mana has been assembling a significant portfolio in downtown Miami’s Flagler District. Over the last 11 years, he has purchased around 80 properties in the area for approximately $600 million, creating one of the largest privately controlled portfolios in the urban core. He also helped lead and fund the Flagler District beautification project.Mana’s broader strategy is framed as a One America vision of connecting the Americas, with Miami as a hub. Downtown is about something bigger than Wynwood, he says, describing Miami as an opportunity to become the economic and innovation capital connecting North America and Latin America. His Mana Tech division aims to attract technology companies and entrepreneurs to Miami, while Mana Fashion is building infrastructure to connect designers and manufacturers with buyers and international markets.The Wynwood sale, while significant, is not the end of Mana’s involvement in Miami. He still controls a large portfolio in Allapattah and continues to invest in downtown. For Mana, the sale is a passing of the torch, allowing someone else to build on what he started and take it even further.A new chapter for a changing neighbourhoodThe $1.1 billion sale of Mana Wynwood marks a turning point for a district that has evolved from abandoned warehouses to a cultural destination and now to a planned centre for education and innovation. Ken Griffin’s purchase clears the way for Carnegie Mellon University Miami, a project that could bring thousands of students, faculty and staff to the area over the next decade. The transaction is a reminder of how quickly urban neighbourhoods can change when long-term investment meets strategic vision.For Moishe Mana, the sale validates a 16-year effort to build an ecosystem around art, culture and community. For Ken Griffin and Carnegie Mellon, it represents an opportunity to add another layer to that ecosystem through education, technology and innovation. As construction begins in 2027, Wynwood’s next chapter will be shaped by a university campus that aims to become a major research and workforce hub in South Florida.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Jason Scott Lee bought 25 acres of damaged Hawaiian land littered with car parts and paint cans; the Hollywood actor built a simple home, grew his own food and worked to bring back the rainforest
articles.summary: Hollywood actor Jason Scott Lee once stepped away from the pressures of celebrity life to embrace a radically simpler existence on a 25-acre farm in
articles.body: Hollywood actor Jason Scott Lee once stepped away from the pressures of celebrity life to embrace a radically simpler existence on a 25-acre farm in Hawaii, where he grew taro, raised chickens and pursued natural farming. An archival report also documented how the Dragon: The Bruce Lee Story star sought to balance acting with environmental and community work.In an older report originally published by the Honolulu Star-Bulletin, Jason Scott Lee opened up about his decision to simplify his lifestyle rather than remain tied to the financial demands and expectations of Hollywood.The actor, who rose to prominence in the 1990s through films including Dragon: The Bruce Lee Story, Rapa Nui, Map of the Human Heart and The Jungle Book, had reached a point where he wanted greater control over his career and personal life."I want to work when I want to, on films that I want to, and not have to pay for a lifestyle that doesn't do anything except obligate me to the machine," Lee said, according to the archival report.The story recalled an incident in Florida in which Lee was discussing Hollywood, money and lifestyles with friends when another actress spoke about a $90,000 Mercedes-Benz she had recently acquired. Lee contrasted that lifestyle with his own desire to live more simply.Jason Scott Lee's 25-acre Hawaii farmAccording to the Honolulu Star-Bulletin report, Lee had purchased 25 acres in Volcano, Hawaii, several years earlier. Much of the land had been deforested and contained debris, including old paint cans and car parts.With the help of a friend, Lee built a modest two-room home on the property. The house had no conventional electricity, hot water or flush toilet. The actor spent much of his time living on the land, embracing a lifestyle far removed from the luxury often associated with Hollywood celebrities.The home used a 12-volt battery for electricity, while a solar panel powered a water pump. A propane tank supplied hot water, and Lee cooked on a wood-burning stove. He even used an old horse trough as a bathtub.The actor grew taro and raised chickensLee's Hawaii lifestyle centred on self-sufficiency, farming and environmental conservation. The report said he grew taro and raised chickens while bartering for other supplies when necessary.His approach to agriculture was influenced by Japanese farmer and philosopher Masanobu Fukuoka, whose philosophy of natural farming rejected intensive tilling and chemical-based agriculture.Lee also worked to restore parts of his property that had been deforested. He collected koa seeds from the surrounding forest and replanted them on his land as part of his efforts to bring back the forest canopy."I want to bring the canopy back," Lee said, according to the report.Jason Scott Lee balanced Hollywood with life in HawaiiAlthough Lee stepped away from the traditional Hollywood lifestyle, he did not completely abandon acting.The actor continued to select film projects that he felt had meaning while earning enough to support his Hawaii-based lifestyle. His credits from that period included the historical epic Nomad and Only the Brave.Lee described his existence as having "one foot in Hollywood and the other in a jungle.""For some people in Hollywood, their soul dies," he said, according to the Honolulu Star-Bulletin account. "You're dependent on so many things: recognition so you can get the next job ... the next movie to pay off your big house and your big car. It's a choice."Jason Scott Lee created Pu Mu for arts and environmental workLee also envisioned turning his Hawaii property, which he called Pu Mu, into a small performing arts centre where socially conscious plays, workshops and classes could be staged.The name Pu Mu was described in the report as representing "simplicity" and "nothingness."At the time of the report, Lee had brought together actors to work on a production while also helping farm part of the property. His broader vision combined theatre, agriculture, environmental conservation and community.The actor explained that his mother and late father had played an important role in shaping his outlook. He credited his mother's compassion and his father's tenacity as major influences on his approach to life.Jason Scott Lee said his life felt completeLee's decision to live simply was not presented as a rejection of acting itself. Rather, he said he had found a way to pursue film work on his own terms while maintaining the lifestyle he wanted in Hawaii."This right here," Lee said while referring to a koa sprout, "is the world that allows me to stand the other one."He added that he would return to Hollywood for film work before going back home to grow, fish, read and work on his theatre projects."My life is pretty complete at Pu Mu," Lee said, according to the archival Honolulu Star-Bulletin report.You use AI every day. articles.title: FBI foils alleged ISIS-linked attack plot at Mall of America by 18-year-old
articles.summary: The FBI thwarted an alleged terror attack at Minnesota’s Mall of America after an 18-year-old suspect agreed to buy an AK-47 rifle and ammunition from an
articles.body: The FBI thwarted an alleged terror attack at Minnesota’s Mall of America after an 18-year-old suspect agreed to buy an AK-47 rifle and ammunition from an undercover agent, US authorities said Wednesday.Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud was arrested Tuesday in a public park in Richfield after paying $600 for a Norinco AK-47 and about 200 rounds of ammunition, according to a federal criminal complaint. The undercover FBI employee was posing as a member of ISIS, according to news agency AP.Mohamud is accused of planning to attack the mall in Bloomington on October 24, when a Hmong arts celebration was scheduled to take place. In messages exchanged with an FBI confidential informant, he repeatedly expressed his intention to kill non-Muslims at the shopping centre, according to the complaint.US Attorney Daniel Rosen said the FBI had detected and disrupted the alleged plan before Mohamud could carry it out.“This was a radicalized young man who needed to be watched,” Rosen said, praising the investigation. Agents “were able to detect a threat, and disrupt it, before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people.”Teen had been under FBI investigation since 2024The FBI first became aware of Mohamud in December 2024, the same month the confidential source began exchanging messages with him, according to the complaint. By May 2025, agents had become concerned enough to visit his home.Mohamud's mother told investigators that he had not yet returned from school and contacted his father. His father declined to speak to the agents and said he would provide their contact details to his lawyer, the complaint said.Mohamud later expressed admiration for recent terror attacks and an interest in travelling to Somalia to join ISIS.He ultimately decided he could not afford the trip and instead planned to attack the Mall of America, the complaint said.As per CNN, court records also described Mohamud as appearing to admire other terrorist-related mass-casualty attacks, including the Bondi Beach shooting in Australia and the New Orleans attack in January 2025.Arrest followed purchase of rifle and ammunitionFederal officials said Mohamud knowingly received the firearm and ammunition to commit a felony and a federal crime of terrorism, according to the complaint.He appeared in federal court in St Paul on Wednesday wearing a yellow jail uniform. It was not immediately known whether he had an attorney who could comment on his behalf, and AP said it could not immediately identify family members for comment.Rosen said Mohamud is an American-born US citizen of Somali descent. He also urged parents to take seriously any indication that their children may be becoming radicalised.“What I would say to parents all over Minnesota, and all over America: If you get any indication — especially if you hear from federal law enforcement — that your son or daughter is being radicalized, to the point where federal law enforcement wants to come and give you that warning, those are warnings that ought to be heeded,” Rosen said.Tens of thousands of people of Somali descent live in Minnesota, with refugees beginning to arrive in the state in the 1990s. Several people from the community have been charged over the years with attempting to join ISIS or other terror groups.Mohamud has been charged with planning a mass-casualty attack in support of ISIS later this month.You use AI every day. articles.title: NIA court rejects bail plea of separatist Shabir Shah in 1996 funeral violence case
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: A Jammu NIA court has rejected the bail application of Hurriyat Conference member Shabir Ahmad Shah in connection with a 30-year-old case of mob
articles.body: SRINAGAR: A Jammu NIA court has rejected the bail application of Hurriyat Conference member Shabir Ahmad Shah in connection with a 30-year-old case of mob violence during a terrorist’s funeral procession in Srinagar, observing that there is “a well-founded apprehension” that if released, he is likely to continue such activities “to the detriment of national security and public order”.Dismissing Shah’s application Tuesday, special judge Prem Sagar said his enlargement on bail at this stage can prejudice fair conduct of the trial and “may adversely affect the confidence and security of the protected witnesses”.An FIR was registered on July 17, 1996, following large-scale violence during a funeral procession in Srinagar. An unruly mob led by Shah, late Syed Ali Shah Geelani, late Abdul Gani Lone and other separatists carried the body of slain terrorist Hilal Ahmad Beigh towards Eidgah, raising anti-India and pro-Pakistan slogans.The mob turned violent when police attempted to regulate the procession. Instigated by the inflammatory speeches of Shah and other Hurriyat functionaries, it resorted to heavy stone-pelting and attacked the cops. According to NIA, armed terrorists also blended in with the procession and fired indiscriminately on the police personnel.In April this year, the ministry of home affairs handed over the investigation to NIA, which re-registered a case.During the bail hearing, Shah said that for 30 years, no step was taken to proceed against him. “A stale investigation resurrected without explanation ... cannot justify the deprivation of personal liberty,” he said. The revival of the 1996 FIR was only aimed at preventing his release following the bail granted by the Supreme Court in March 2025 in a 2017 terror funding case, he argued. Shah was arrested in the terror funding case in June 2019.Besides, he argued that co-accused who were allegedly part of the very same procession had been granted bail long back.Concurring with NIA, which opposed the bail plea, the court said that “every case under UAPA has serious consequences” and has to be examined “vis-a-vis the nature of allegations, centrality of the role, protected witnesses, risk of intimidation, possibility of reactivation of networks etc”. It also rejected the grounds of parity with the other accused persons.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Rs 90 LPA in Bengaluru or $300k in San Jose: Redditor asks if it's wiser to move to US on an L1 visa
articles.summary: The dollar-rupee conversion is not always a straight calculation, especially when there are issues of lifestyle and career growth to be taken into account.
articles.body: The dollar-rupee conversion is not always a straight calculation, especially when there are issues of lifestyle and career growth to be taken into account. $300k is more than Rs 90 lakh mathematically but a Redditor said he's unable to make up his mind whether he should move to the US on a $300k offer in San Jose or whether he should continue in Bengaluru, where he is getting Rs 90 LPA. For context, he said that it would not be on an H-1B visa but an L-1, in which he will be transferred from India to the US to work for the same company. It's a startup that he had been working for for around two years. He added that he is a 36-year-old married man with no loans, no kids -- and his wife works part-time.The man said that career-wise he feels saturated in Bengaluru, so much so that he would call it borderline lazy as he also wondered whether he had any scope to grow more in Bengaluru. He said he spoke to his San Francisco region friends who dismissed his interest in taking the plunge but he showed a keen interest in exploring a US career and he said he researched the cost of living and concluded that he could be saving around $5k-6k per month in the US.The Bengaluru man was looking for genuine advice and the Reddit community was divided. Some people advised him to choose Bengaluru over San Jose and explained that $300K in the US would actually be a pay cut from his Rs 90LPA salary. They also reminded him that since he would be on an L1 visa, he would be tied to his company and if he's fired, it would be a lot different than getting fired in India.But many Redditors said that, without any kids, he was in the best position to explore the US life and culture and business growth and in the worst-case scenario, he would just have to come back to India -- but with dollar savings from the US. Some said they made a similar decision and never regretted moving to the US.What is an L- visa?The L-1 visa is a US work visa that lets a company transfer an employee from its foreign office to a related US office. This visa comes with a maximum stay period. Under current regulations, an L-1 worker whose employment ends can get a maximum 60-day grace period, or until the end of the existing authorised stay, whichever is earlier. But unlike H-1B, L-1 visa holders can not just find another US company and transfer their visa. A new employer would generally need to qualify for an L-1 relationship with a foreign entity and you would need to independently satisfy the L-1 requirements. In many ordinary situations, therefore, you'd need to move to another visa category or leave the US.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Jewish student sues New York school on Oct 7 anniversary over 'relentless antisemitic harassment'
articles.summary: Student Sophie Shabot alleged antisemitic assault and harassment at The New School's Parsons School of Design in a new lawsuit by The Lawfare Project.
articles.body: The Lawfare Project announced on the third anniversary of the deadly Oct. 7 Hamas attacks on Israel that it filed a lawsuit against The New School on behalf of a Jewish Israeli-American student it alleged faced "relentless antisemitic harassment, intimidation, and physical assault" as a student at the New York university. According to the legal group, New School student Sophie Shabot faced numerous instances of name-calling, intimidation and obstruction based on her religion and support for Israel at the Parsons School of Design. She was reportedly called names like "Zio b----" and "baby killer" and prevented from entering the University Center. In another instance, protesters allegedly vandalized and disrupted a Hillel event featuring an Israeli speaker in 2024. Shabot was among several Jewish students who were trapped in a dean's office as a group of protesters attempted to have them turn over the speaker. JEWISH CAMPUS LIFE AT A ‘CROSSING POINT’ AS STUDENTS WEIGH ANTISEMITISM RISKS, NEW REPORT SHOWS According to The Lawfare Project, university officials failed to stop the harassment against Shabot and other Jewish students and even "at times rewarded those responsible." "There is no question in my mind that the New School violated its Title VI obligations and other obligations under the law in not intervening and taking meaningful action to stop the antisemitic, anti-Israeli harassment that my plaintiff endured while she was at the New School," Lawfare Project director of litigation Ziporah Reich told Fox News Digital. Reich, who also filed the lawsuit, added that more often than not, Jewish students like Shabot were the ones who faced consequences at universities following antisemitic actions by other students. "If the pro-Hamas protesters are essentially threatening your physical safety when you're trying to have a Jewish event, let's just shut down the event to make sure you're safe. When a group of pro-Hamas protesters occupy a space in which you're supposed to have an event, let's just move you somewhere else to a smaller, less accommodating place. In other words, she was bearing the brunt of the consequences for the negative harassment of the offenders," Reich said. JEWISH UCLA STUDENTS BEATEN WITH STICKS, PEPPER SPRAYED AND KNOCKED OUT BY ANTI-ISRAEL CAMPUS MOB: LAWSUIT Reich also acknowledged the significance of filing the lawsuit Wednesday on the anniversary of the attacks that killed more than 1,200 people in Israel and led to more than 250 people being abducted. "It's extremely important for the Jewish community to recognize that what happened immediately after Oct. 7 didn't end immediately after Oct. 7 because the harassment of Jewish students and Jews everywhere has continued and even if it has lessened to some extent in certain universities, it has not gone away. It's essentially in a quiet period where we know that at any minute it can rear its ugly head again. These students are activists without a cause," Reich said. The lawsuit brings claims under Title VI, New York state and city civil and human rights laws and claims for breach of contract and negligent infliction of emotional distress. It is seeking damages, statutory penalties, attorneys’ fees and costs, and other relief and demands a jury trial. articles.title: A Florida billionaire bought an 8.4-acre oceanfront estate for $80 million in 2021; five years later, the vacant property is asking $165 million, with 562 feet of Atlantic frontage
articles.summary: Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison is putting one of his most spectacular Florida properties back on the market, and this time the asking price is $165
articles.body: Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison is putting one of his most spectacular Florida properties back on the market, and this time the asking price is $165 million. The Wall Street Journal first reported the planned relisting, while The Real Deal and Realtor.com provided additional details about the property, its history and the latest listing. Ellison bought the 8.4-acre oceanfront estate in North Palm Beach for $80 million in 2021, meaning the current asking price is more than double what he paid five years ago. The property, known as the Seminole Beach Estate, sits inside the gated Seminole Landing community, next to the Seminole Golf Club. Rather than being a typical luxury-home sale, however, the listing is largely about the extraordinary piece of land itself. The estate is among the largest oceanfront parcels in Palm Beach County, with roughly 562 to 563 feet of direct Atlantic frontage, depending on the source.A property built for a major redevelopmentEllison acquired the estate through an entity linked to him in April 2021. At the time, his plan was reportedly to demolish the existing Mediterranean-style residence and create something new on the expansive oceanfront site. That never happened. The existing house remained, and the property was subsequently offered for sale in 2022 with a $145 million asking price. It failed to find a buyer and was eventually taken off the market. Now, instead of reducing the price, Ellison has returned with an even higher figure: $165 million.The new asking price would represent a 106% increase over Ellison’s original purchase price. The Real Deal reported that it also amounts to more than $10,000 per square foot and roughly $19.6 million per acre, making it a record-level ask for North Palm Beach.Inside the oceanfront compoundThe existing residence, built in 1991, spans more than 16,000 square feet. Realtor.com lists seven bedrooms and eight bathrooms, while other property reports describe additional half-baths and extensive supporting spaces. The house also comes with a four-car garage, pool terrace, tennis court, wine room and a VIP guest suite.But the home’s size may not be the property’s biggest selling point. The estate offers direct access to the Atlantic and an unusually large stretch of beachfront, making it particularly attractive to a buyer interested in building a custom compound rather than simply moving into the existing house. The parcel also has room for a private helipad, a rare feature even among South Florida’s most expensive estates. It sits within a community with around-the-clock security, adding another layer of privacy to the already secluded oceanfront setting.Why Ellison may be moving onThe sale comes as Ellison continues to concentrate significant real estate holdings farther south in Palm Beach County. In 2022, an Ellison-controlled company acquired a roughly 15-acre ocean-to-Intracoastal estate in Manalapan for $173 million. This year, he has continued expanding that property with an additional land purchase reported at about $35 million.His Palm Beach County portfolio is already extensive. In 2023, he reportedly spent nearly $10 million acquiring eight homes in Boynton Beach to house staff connected with his Manalapan operation. That makes the decision to part with the North Palm Beach property less surprising. Rather than developing another enormous residence, Ellison appears to be concentrating his South Florida real estate footprint around the much larger Manalapan compound.Whether someone will pay $165 million for the Seminole Landing estate remains to be seen. For now, the figure is an asking price rather than a completed sale. But if it attracts a buyer anywhere near that number, Ellison’s five-year-old $80 million purchase could become one of North Palm Beach’s most significant luxury-property transactions.You use AI every day. articles.body: BIRMINGHAM, Ala. - Alabama could have one of its most important players this weekend against Georgia, even though he suffered a broken arm last week against Mississippi State. articles.title: In 1905, William and Elizabeth Kent paid $45,000 for 611 acres of California redwood forest; after a reservoir threat, they donated about 295 acres and the land became Muir Woods National Monument in 1908
articles.summary: Explore the inspiring story of how William and Elizabeth Kent transformed a threatened California redwood forest into the iconic Muir Woods National Monument in 1908, emphasizing their pivotal roles in conservation.
articles.body: A stretch of California redwood forest that could have been logged and turned into a reservoir became one of the country's best-known protected forests after William and Elizabeth Kent chose to give much of their land to the federal government.The Kents bought 611 acres in Redwood Canyon in 1905 for $45,000, as surrounding forests were being cleared for timber and commercial use. Three years later, they donated about 295 acres to the federal government, and President Theodore Roosevelt proclaimed the land Muir Woods National Monument, according to the National Park Service (NPS).The decision followed a dispute over plans to build a reservoir in the canyon and came after years of efforts by conservationists to protect its redwoods.A family with roots in CaliforniaWilliam Kent came from a wealthy family with roots in Connecticut. His father, Albert Kent, came from a prosperous farming family, attended Yale, and built his fortune through businesses and real estate investments.The Kent family moved to Marin County in 1871. William grew up around the landscape near the Golden Gate and developed an appreciation for the area's natural environment.At Yale, William met Elizabeth Thacher, whose father was a Latin professor at the university. The couple later married and had seven children and 10 grandchildren.They eventually settled in Chicago, where William took control of his father's businesses and entered local politics. By 1903, however, an economic depression had affected the family's finances.That year, William and Elizabeth travelled to Marin County to visit relatives. During the trip, a friend took them to Redwood Canyon and encouraged them to buy the grove and protect its redwoods.The couple initially hesitated but eventually purchased the property for $45,000, a heavily discounted price intended to make preservation possible, as per the NPS.Reservoir plan puts the forest at riskThe threat to the redwoods became more immediate in 1907.The North Coast Water Company held water rights in the canyon and sought to develop a reservoir by damming the creek. The proposal put the future of the redwood grove at risk and led to a legal dispute with the Kents.The conflict came after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, which destroyed much of the city and left large areas in need of rebuilding. Pressure to use redwood timber increased as reconstruction got underway.Public interest in the forest had already grown through conservation campaigns and improved access to Mount Tamalpais. The Mount Tamalpais Railroad, in which William Kent was a major shareholder, also opened a branch into the redwood grove in 1907, allowing visitors to reach the forest by railway.Rather than sell the property or allow the reservoir project to proceed, Kent sought federal protection for the land.He approached Gifford Pinchot, the head of the newly established US Forest Service, who brought the dispute to President Theodore Roosevelt.295 acres become a national monumentThe recently enacted Antiquities Act gave the president the authority to establish national monuments through presidential proclamation.In January 1908, Roosevelt accepted about 295 acres of the Kents' property and proclaimed it Muir Woods National Monument.It became the seventh national monument and the first created from land donated to the federal government by a private individual.Kent could have asked for the monument to carry his family's name. Instead, he requested that it be named after his friend and fellow conservationist John Muir.The donation also brought the dispute over the proposed reservoir to an end.Elizabeth Kent's role was largely overlookedAlthough William Kent is often associated with the creation of Muir Woods, Elizabeth Thacher Kent was also a co-owner of the property and played a role in the family's business, philanthropic, and civic activities.Elizabeth came from a politically connected family and was the great-granddaughter of Roger Sherman, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States.The Kents' political records were more complicated than their conservation legacy. William later served in Congress and supported restrictions aimed at excluding Chinese and Japanese immigrants from the United States. Elizabeth was also active in politics and became involved in causes beyond her husband's public career.Their conservation work therefore formed only one part of their wider public lives.A forest protected for more than a centuryMuir Woods has remained a national monument since Roosevelt's 1908 proclamation. The site marked its centennial in 2008, a century after the Kents' donation.Later conservation projects have focused on protecting the forest's ecosystem, restoring Redwood Creek and improving conditions for species including coho salmon, steelhead trout and the California red-legged frog.A 2014 BioBlitz brought together more than 320 volunteer scientists, along with thousands of families, teachers and students, to document plants, insects, mammals, birds and other species in Muir Woods and the surrounding Golden Gate National Recreation Area.The forest has also introduced measures to manage tourism and reduce pressure on its fragile resources, including a parking reservation and shuttle system.You use AI every day. articles.title: Anti-CEC protests: Opposition, police face off again; Rahul Gandhi says won’t stop till Gyanesh quits
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Opposition INDIA bloc members on Wednesday travelled by buses from their lunch meeting in Connaught Place towards Jantar Mantar, seeking to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Opposition INDIA bloc members on Wednesday travelled by buses from their lunch meeting in Connaught Place towards Jantar Mantar, seeking to protest and demand CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. But for the second day in a row, Delhi Police stalled their agitation, detaining them less than 1km from their intended “flash protest” site.“We are not going to stop protesting till CEC Gyanesh Kumar resigns,” said Rahul Gandhi, who was detained along with 90 others, including MPs and workers, after hours of confrontation with police in front of Shangri-La hotel. They were taken to Barakhamba police station and released later around 8:30 pm.My target is 100 FIRs against me. Every FIR a medal: RahulLater, Congress issued a directive to all its state, block and district committees, to hold “massive demonstrations” to protest the police action to prevent the INDIA bloc from holding a protest at Jantar Mantar. “Congress declares today as a black day for Indian democracy,” it stated.The joint opposition made it clear that their protest will continue undeterred and a bigger protest plan is in the works for Thursday.However, Delhi Police said restrictions imposed under BNSS’s Section 163 were in force in the New Delhi area, which is why the protesters were detained. “As Section 163 is in force here… protest marches or demonstrations are not allowed without permission,” DCP Sachin Sharma said.It all began with Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge hosting INDIA bloc MPs for lunch at a restaurant in Janpath, which began around 1.30pm and where the gathering was informed about a plan to continue the protest against CEC, this time with a march to Jantar Mantar for a demonstration.Members, including Congress’s Rahul, KC Venugopal and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, John Brittas (CPM), P Sandosh Kumar (CPI), Manoj Jha (RJD), Derek O’Brien (TMC), Thol Thirumavalavan (VCK), emerged from the restaurant and announced the protest plan. MPs of JMM and IUML also joined them.They headed for buses waiting for them to leave. But the administration had stationed police in heavy numbers at Janpath, which, coupled with the gathering of onlookers and rush of political workers, made it difficult for the buses to move. Some Congress MPs and functionaries climbed on the roof of one of the buses, waving Tricolour. The MPs were forced to dismount from the buses in front of the hotel, where they were surrounded by police. Priyanka, Raja Warring and Deepender Hooda sat down on the road along with some workers, even as the cops continued to request Rahul to get into a bus. Cops finally picked up Rahul and took him away in a mini van. Similarly, Priyanka, who was lying on the street clutching a copy of the Constitution, along with other women workers of her party, was removed.Police claimed that some protesters attacked their personnel. A sub-inspector alleged protesters bit him and tore his uniform. Police are also analysing mobile-phone videos following allegations that police personnel, including women, were assaulted near Jantar Mantar.Kharge and Rahul said the opposition will continue with its protests till CEC resigns. On an FIR being registered against him for entering Akashvani Bhavan premises and staging an eight-hour sit-in Tuesday, Rahul said, “I have 45 FIRs against me. My target is that there should be 100 FIRs against me. Every FIR against me is a medal for me.” Rahul said the opposition decided to demonstrate at Jantar Mantar, which is the designated protest site, as govt told them that dharna couldn’t be held at places like Election Commission.While some of Congress’ allies were absent from the lunch, party spokesperson Jairam Ramesh said the decision for lunch was taken late Tuesday night, and the absence was understandable.On Samajwadi Party, O’Brien said there was a minor miscommunication, which was addressed swiftly, and Samajwadi Party will join the protest Thursday.Sources said Congress had reached out to certain opposition parties to make it clear there was some misunderstanding and the decision to enter Akashwani Bhavan Tuesday was taken on the spur. Left and TMC functionaries were also dismissive of any lingering differences.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: Hasan “HasanAbi” Piker has accused fellow Twitch streamer Zack “Asmongold” of racism after Asmongold shared a highly controversial view on France’s ongoing student protests. During a livestream on October 6, Asmongold publicly argued that immigrants and their families should be removed from France and said protesters with immigrant parents or grandparents should not be considered native French. Hasan later reacted to the remarks on his own stream. He called Asmongold a racist and described his argument as “pure, vulgar white nationalism.” As of October 7, Asmongold had not publicly responded to Hasan’s remarks so far.Asmongold shares controversial view on France protestsFrance has been dealing with growing student protests over teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and poor school conditions. Reports from AP and other outlets said the protests have spread across the country. Students have called for better resources and improvements to schools.While discussing the protests on October 6, Asmongold offered a much broader response. He argued that immigrants who he believes are responsible for problems in France should be removed from the country.He said:“The solution to end this is to take every single negative taxpayer, who is not a native Frenchman or a native European, and remove every single one of them from the country with the military.”Asmongold also said their families should be removed with them. He added that he would shoot anyone who became violent during such an operation.He then questioned whether protesters with immigrant parents or grandparents should be considered French.“These people are not native French. Their parents are immigrants. Their grandparents are immigrants. They’re not from France. They’re not Europeans. These are foreigners.”Asmongold also argued that having French paperwork or being born in France does not automatically make someone French.His comments focused on who should be considered French rather than only addressing the education issues that led to the protests.HasanAbi accuses Asmongold of racismHasanAbi later watched and reacted to Asmongold’s comments during his own livestream. He focused on the streamer’s argument about immigrants and described it as an example of fascism.Hasan said fascist movements can grow during periods of economic instability. He then pointed to the actual demands behind the protests.“By the way, what they’re protesting is for, like, more funding for schools, so they actually have teachers - substitute teachers - more funding for schools so that the walls don’t collapse while they’re in the classroom.”Hasan then directly accused Asmongold of racism.“Asmongold is a ****** racist. This is pure, vulgar white nationalism. That is the only reason why he thinks that these people are not French.”Hasan’s comments were a response to Asmongold’s statements rather than a separate discussion about the wider French protest movement.The protests themselves have continued to grow. On October 6, hundreds of thousands of people took part in demonstrations across France, according to Le Monde. The protests have included demands involving overcrowded classrooms, staff shortages and poor school infrastructure.As of October 7, Asmongold had not publicly addressed HasanAbi’s accusations. articles.title: Cardiff cancer survivor 'screamed at' by airport staff over stoma supplies
articles.summary: Paul Scanlon says airport travel can be "degrading and humiliating" for people with stomas.
articles.body:
A cancer survivor said he was screamed at by airport security staff and "made to feel like a criminal" after trying to retrieve his stoma supplies from his luggage.

Paul Scanlon, from Cardiff, has had a stoma for nearly four years after being diagnosed with stage three bowel cancer and said he had suffered "degrading" and "humiliating" treatment at UK airports.

Now, a charity wants better training for airport staff so people with stomas are treated with "dignity" and "respect".

The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) said airports must ensure staff have disability awareness training and that security officers were expected to treat people in a "sensitive and understanding" way.

Travel has always been something 57-year-old Paul has enjoyed - even more so since his diagnosis.

"When you've gone through what we've gone through over the last four years, it makes you really appreciate that you can go away," he said.

Paul was initially reluctant to have a stoma - an opening in the stomach that allows waste to leave the body and into a bag - after having his large bowel removed due to the size of his tumours.

"It's having your bum on your belly and it's not for the faint-hearted, but it's a lifesaver," he said.

"I don't know if you 100% come to terms with it. You end up just living with it."

What Paul did not expect to have to come to terms with was hostility at airports.

Paul said he was once told by security to remove his stoma bag at a UK airport - something he is unable to do.

His most recent experience was at Cardiff Airport while travelling on holiday with his wife Deborah, and their friends.

He said he was "screamed" at after trying to remove his bag of stoma supplies from the conveyor belt after security screening.

"This very large gentleman started shouting and screaming: 'You can't touch that bag, leave it alone, get away'.

"He kept walking towards me, shouting and screaming. He and his colleague escorted me, one flank to either side, into an interview room where I was searched.

"Everyone can see going through that airport. Anyone can see. You're just made to feel like a criminal."

Paul said he was "mortified" and, while understanding the need to keep everyone safe, felt there was a lack of "dignity, compassion and empathy".

During the incident, Deborah and their friends were also left waiting without any explanation of where he had been taken.

"If you're in that job, you should be looking at treating people with respect," he said.

Cardiff Airport said, when additional screening was required, passengers can be offered a private search room "to help ensure the process is carried out with dignity and discretion".

It also said its teams had done training "to help them better understand the experiences of people living with a stoma and ensure any necessary screening is carried out sensitively, respectfully and appropriately".

A spokesperson said that while the company did not comment on individual cases, anyone unhappy with an experience was encouraged to contact the airport so it can review what happened.

These experiences have left Paul reluctant to travel through airports.

"It's completely changed my thought process of going on holiday. I don't want to fly," he said.

His next holiday will be a cruise leaving from Southampton, allowing him to avoid the stress he associates with flying.

"I've got next year to get through and I'll be hopefully cancer free. You know, we've got loads of life left in us and we still want to go on holiday."

Paul's experience is not unique, according to the Ileostomy and Internal Pouch Association (IA).

It has a survey open which has received 70 responses and identified 16 different UK airports where people have reported negative stoma-related incidents.

IA chief executive officer Lisa Barker said people were being forced to make a choice between living with a stoma and getting to travel, and that airport security procedures caused "a lot of stress and anxiety".

The organisation offers a free service providing travel certificates explaining a person's condition which can be shown to airport staff, but Lisa wants that information translated into better understanding.

"What we want is that once that information is shared, the knowledge about that then enables them to have a dignified process," she said.

Emma Greenwood is an internal pouch nurse specialist and has a stoma - she said she had faced similar problems at airports.

"If you're spoken to abruptly or fairly aggressively in some situations, it can naturally be quite upsetting and it can have a negative impact on your holiday," she said.

Emma said people with pouches could be self-conscious and sensitive and may be particularly concerned about being embarrassed during security checks.

"It's a quick win to be kind to someone," she said.

"It's not a massive adjustment that the majority of people are asking for."

The CAA said it placed obligations on airports "to ensure their staff receive disability awareness training" and expected security officers to engage with passengers in "a sensitive and understanding manner".

Disability Wales said the issue was not limited to people with stomas.

Access to politics policy officer Kat Watkins, who has brittle bone disease, said she had experienced several negative incidents including damage to her wheelchair and being left on the plane for an hour while waiting for assistance.

She said Disability Wales wanted air travel to be "made more equitable for disabled people".

The CAA said it strongly believed that "everyone should have access to air travel" and continues to "work closely with organisations and charities representing disabled passengers to ensure guidance to airports and passengers is clear and concise".

articles.title: In 2025, Swiss startup installed 48 removable solar panels between active railway tracks; today, 11,000 trains have passed over the 100-metre plant, generating more than 16,000 kWh
articles.summary: A Swiss startup has spent more than a year testing an unusual way to generate renewable energy: placing removable solar panels directly between the rails
articles.body: A Swiss startup has spent more than a year testing an unusual way to generate renewable energy: placing removable solar panels directly between the rails of an active railway line.At a pilot project in Buttes, Switzerland, more than 11,000 trains have already travelled over the installation, while the system has generated more than 16,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity since May 2025.According to SWI Swissinfo, the installation has remained stable and has not interfered with train operations or railway maintenance during the pilot.The project is being developed by Swiss startup Sun-Ways, which installed 48 photovoltaic panels along a 100-metre section of railway in April 2025. Sun-Ways describes the project as the world's first removable solar power plant installed on an active railway line.Solar panels fit into the space between railway tracksThe concept is strikingly simple: instead of buying land for a conventional solar farm, Sun-Ways uses the narrow strip of space that already exists between two railway rails.The 48 panels installed at Buttes have a combined capacity of around 18 kilowatts. According to pv magazine, the system was designed specifically for railway infrastructure and can be removed when maintenance work needs to be carried out.The panels are installed between the rails rather than alongside the railway. Trains therefore pass directly over them.That makes the project different from conventional railway solar installations, which typically place panels on railway buildings, embankments or nearby land.Sun-Ways' patented system is designed to be removable, allowing railway workers to access the track when necessary.More than 11,000 trains have passed over the solar panelsThe first results from the Buttes pilot suggest the concept can withstand regular railway traffic.SWI Swissinfo reported that more than 11,000 trains have travelled over the installation since it was commissioned. Trains travelling along the section can reach speeds of around 90 kilometres per hour, or about 56 mph.Despite the repeated traffic, the solar installation has remained stable.“We have achieved our objectives, both in terms of railway safety and electricity production,” Sun-Ways founder Joseph Scuderi told Swissinfo.The project has also generated more than 16,000 kWh of electricity since May 2025.Swissinfo reported that the output is equivalent to the average annual electricity consumption of roughly three to four Swiss households.The installation was temporarily stopped for about a month because of snow and planned technical work, but the project continued to demonstrate that photovoltaic panels could operate in the challenging environment of an active railway.The panels can be removed for maintenanceOne of the biggest questions surrounding solar panels on railway tracks is whether they could obstruct routine maintenance.Railway operators regularly need access to tracks for inspections, repairs, sleeper replacement and other infrastructure work.Sun-Ways designed its system around that problem.According to SWI Swissinfo, the panels can be disconnected and removed using specialised equipment when railway work is required. A module containing three panels and covering about six metres can reportedly be removed in roughly 10 minutes.That means the solar installation does not have to remain permanently fixed to the track.The removable design is also one of the key features Sun-Ways hopes will make the technology suitable for railway networks in other countries.Trains may help keep the panels cleanDust and dirt are another challenge for any solar installation.Solar panels become less efficient when their surfaces become heavily covered with dust, potentially requiring regular cleaning.Sun-Ways initially considered developing a mechanical cleaning system using a brush attached to trains.But according to Scuderi's comments reported by Swissinfo, the company found that trains themselves can create airflow capable of helping remove dust from the panels.The Buttes project is being used to study several other issues, including soiling, glare, railway maintenance and the interaction between the photovoltaic installation and railway infrastructure.The absence of reported problems with train operations is significant because railway authorities would need to be satisfied that the technology does not create additional safety risks before approving large-scale installations.Switzerland's railway network could generate significant electricityThe 100-metre Buttes installation represents only a tiny fraction of Switzerland's railway network.Sun-Ways estimates that suitable sections of Switzerland's approximately 5,320-kilometre railway network could potentially be equipped with its technology.According to SWI Swissinfo, the company estimates that such installations could generate as much as 1 billion kWh of electricity annually.Sun-Ways says that amount could be enough to supply around 300,000 Swiss households and represent roughly 2% of Switzerland's electricity consumption.Those figures are company estimates, however, rather than a confirmed national-generation forecast.Not every section of railway would necessarily be suitable. Tunnels, shaded areas, curves, maintenance requirements, railway design and other technical restrictions could limit where solar panels can be installed.Still, the potential is significant because railway lines already occupy long stretches of land.Instead of acquiring new land for solar farms, railway operators could potentially generate electricity using infrastructure corridors that already exist.Railway solar attracts international interestThe Buttes pilot has attracted attention well beyond Switzerland.Scuderi previously told pv magazine that railway representatives from countries including Indonesia, Japan and South Korea had shown interest in the technology.In July 2025, Scuderi told pv magazine that a company from Indonesia's railway sector had visited the Swiss installation to verify that the technology was real and operating as claimed.He also said there had been interest from Japan and South Korea, where railway speeds can be considerably higher than those at the Swiss pilot site.That creates another technical challenge.Sun-Ways has said its prototype technology has been validated for trains travelling at speeds of up to 150 km/h, while the Buttes railway operates at significantly lower speeds.Any expansion to high-speed railways would therefore require additional testing and regulatory approval.France's SNCF is now working with Sun-WaysInterest in the technology has also progressed from observation to formal cooperation.In February 2026, France's national railway operator SNCF signed an agreement with Sun-Ways to study the technology and assess whether it could eventually be used on parts of the French railway network.According to SWI Swissinfo, the collaboration gives SNCF access to data and technical information from the Swiss pilot.pv magazine similarly reported that the French railway group was studying the performance and practical implications of installing photovoltaic panels directly between tracks.The partnership is technical and regulatory tests.The pilot is scheduled to continue through 2028The Buttes installation is not yet a full commercial rollout.The pilot is scheduled to continue through April 2028, giving Sun-Ways and railway partners additional time to assess the technology under different weather and operating conditions.Scuderi has indicated that the company wants the strong early results to help accelerate regulatory approval.“We have demonstrated that the solar plant between the rails is safe,” he said, according to the company's reporting of the project. “The sooner we obtain final approval, the sooner our partners abroad will also be able to move forwards.”The remaining pilot period will therefore be important in determining whether the technology can move from a small demonstration project to commercial railway infrastructure.Could railway tracks become solar power plants?The significance of the Sun-Ways project goes beyond its 48 panels.Railways are among the most extensive pieces of infrastructure in many countries. Their tracks stretch through cities, suburbs and rural areas, often creating long corridors where conventional development is difficult.The space between two rails, meanwhile, is normally unused for energy generation.Sun-Ways is attempting to turn that narrow strip into a source of renewable electricity without purchasing additional land or clearing large areas for solar farms.If the technology proves reliable at larger scale, similar systems could potentially be deployed on suitable railway lines around the world.But the Swiss pilot has not yet demonstrated that every railway can accommodate solar panels. articles.body: Flight delays, cancellations and even the drive to terminals can add layers of frustration to already challenging travel experiences. A new analysis looked at some of the busiest airports across the U.S. to determine where travelers may encounter the most stress. articles.title: Queen Elizabeth II opened London Zoo’s Lion Terraces in 1976; 40 years later, she returned to open a new home for endangered Asiatic lions
articles.summary: A royal visit to London Zoo in 2016 completed a circle that had begun 40 years earlier.
articles.body: A royal visit to London Zoo in 2016 completed a circle that had begun 40 years earlier. According to the Zoological Society of London, Queen Elizabeth II opened the Lion Terraces at London Zoo in 1976, then returned in 2016, during her 90th birthday year, to open Land of the Lions, a new conservation breeding centre for Asiatic lions, alongside the then Duke of Edinburgh. ZSL described the 2016 visit as completing a circle of royal engagement spanning decades. The Zoological Society of London, founded in 1826, has maintained close connections with the British Royal Family throughout its history, with the reigning monarch serving as its Royal Patron since the time of William IV.ZSL and the royal family: 2 centuries of royal connections at London ZooThe relationship dates back to the Society's earliest years. King George IV granted ZSL its Royal Charter on 27 March 1829, establishing it as an institution of national importance. In 1831, William IV, ZSL's first official Royal Patron, offered to move the Royal Menagerie from the Tower of London, giving the animals a new home at the Society's scientific zoo. London Zoo had opened in Regent's Park in 1828 and was initially accessible only to ZSL Fellows before eventually opening to the public in 1847.Queen Elizabeth II first visited London Zoo as a child in 1938 with Princess Margaret. After becoming Queen, she returned repeatedly during her 70-year reign. ZSL records visits including her 1976 opening of the Lion Terraces, her 1990 opening of the Lifewatch Centre, and her 1999 opening of the Millennium Conservation Centre. In 2016, she and Prince Philip returned to open Land of the Lions, linking her later visit directly to the lion habitat she had opened 4 decades earlier.Queen Elizabeth's visits to London Zoo: from the Lion Terraces in 1976 to Land of the Lions in 2016Other members of the Royal Family also played significant roles in ZSL's history. Prince Philip, the former Duke of Edinburgh, served as ZSL President from 1960 to 1977 and was instrumental in the establishment of the Institute of Zoology, the Society's scientific research division. He remained an Honorary Fellow from 1977 until his death in 2021. Lord Snowdon, the former husband of Princess Margaret, also left a lasting mark on London Zoo through the Snowdon Aviary. Opened in 1965, it was Britain's first walk-through aviary and was designed by Snowdon with architect Cedric Price and structural engineer Frank Newby. The pioneering structure used aluminium and tension-based engineering and rose to 24 metres at its highest points. ZSL says legend has it that Snowdon incorporated a secret tribute to Princess Margaret into the design, with the walkway forming the shape of an “M” for Margaret when viewed from above. The former aviary has since been restored and reimagined as Monkey Valley, a home for eastern black-and-white colobus monkeys.Prince Philip, Lord Snowdon and King Charles: other royal links to London Zoo and WhipsnadePrince Philip and Queen Elizabeth II also opened Whipsnade Zoo's Centre for Elephant Care in 2017. ZSL describes the visit as one of Prince Philip's final public engagements. The royal connection continued with King Charles III, who first visited London Zoo at 1 year old to see Brumas, a newborn polar bear cub. He returned several times as a child, including when he was about 5, to visit the former Pets Corner, now Animal Adventure. At age 13, he joined ZSL's Exceptional Young Zoologist Club, which was created to encourage children's interest in zoology. His Majesty's Patronage of ZSL was announced in May 2024, continuing the tradition of the reigning monarch serving as the Society's Royal Patron.On 9 July 2026, King Charles III and Queen Camilla visited London Zoo to mark ZSL's 200th anniversary. The visit was Charles's first official engagement as ZSL's Patron and Queen Camilla's first official visit to the Society. Their Majesties met conservationists, scientists, veterinarians, educators and animal-care experts during the visit. From William IV's early patronage and the Royal Family's visits to London Zoo to Queen Elizabeth II's 1976 and 2016 lion openings and King Charles III's 2026 bicentenary visit, the relationship between ZSL and the British Royal Family has spanned 2 centuries.You use AI every day. articles.title: Meet 81-year-old billionaire John Poindexter, who is spending $67 million into reviving a Texas ghost town with just 25 residents
articles.summary: Shafter, Texas, is a former silver-mining town with only about 25 residents today, but billionaire John Poindexter sees a future in its abandoned
articles.body: Shafter, Texas, is a former silver-mining town with only about 25 residents today, but billionaire John Poindexter sees a future in its abandoned buildings and history. His Tidewater and Big Bend Foundation has received nearly $67 million since 2020 and is backing plans to restore parts of the settlement, including its historic church, saloon, general store and post office, as reported by Fortune. About a dozen adobe homes could eventually become accommodation for visitors. The project comes as Presidio County continues to lose population and faces limited services, with residents travelling 19 miles to Presidio for groceries. For Poindexter, the aim is to turn a declining mining town into a place where its past can still be experienced.Inside the Texas ghost town of Shafter where only 25 residents remainShafter sits in Presidio County, close to the Mexican border and about 19 miles from Presidio, where residents currently have to go for groceries. The wider county had an estimated 5,433 residents in 2025, according to US Census Bureau figures. That was 11.4% lower than its 2020 population and well below the 7,818 recorded in 2010.The county is also considerably poorer than the United States as a whole. Its median household income was $43,802, roughly half the national median, while almost one in five residents was living below the poverty line. The population density was only about 1.6 people per square mile.The former mining settlement has roughly 25 residents, according to the Big Bend Sentinel, making any attempt to turn it into a functioning visitor destination a sizeable undertaking.The foundation behind the Shafter projectReportedly, since late 2020, Poindexter's Tidewater and Big Bend Foundation has received nearly $67 million in contributions, based on IRS filings compiled by ProPublica. In the financial year ending in November 2024, the foundation reported $20.6 million in contributions and $62.5 million in net assets. The organisation has increasingly directed its resources towards properties and preservation in the Big Bend region. Shafter is at the centre of that work, with plans that go beyond simply repairing a few old buildings.The proposed development is intended to recreate part of the town's historic character. A restored saloon, general store and post office would form part of the project, while roughly a dozen adobe houses are expected to provide accommodation for visitors.How Shafter’s 1883 silver mine shaped the Texas ghost townShafter's history stretches back to the late 19th century. Its Presidio Mine began operating in 1883 and remained in production until 1942. During that period, the mine produced 35.2 million ounces of silver, according to Mining News Australia, which now owns the mining operation.The mine was the reason the settlement existed in the first place. Once production stopped, so did much of the economic activity that had supported the community. The population declined and buildings were left behind. Poindexter began acquiring properties in Shafter and, by early 2025, was offering to restore the historic church near the town entrance. A restaurant and shop were also being discussed as part of efforts to give the settlement more services and reasons for people to visit.Not every local resident has embraced the plans. There are also basic practical problems to solve before Shafter could support a larger population or visitor economy.Poindexter wants visitors to experience the pastHenry Thompson, an officer of Poindexter's foundation, has compared the concept with Colonial Williamsburg. The Virginia historic district combines preserved buildings with visitor accommodation, allowing people to experience the setting rather than simply view it as a collection of monuments.That comparison has an interesting precedent. John D. Rockefeller Jr. began acquiring properties in Williamsburg in the 1920s as part of a restoration project that eventually transformed the former colonial capital into a major historic attraction. Rockefeller initially kept his involvement quiet before committing $5 million to the restoration.Poindexter is taking a much more visible approach. He hosted around 200 guests in Shafter over Labor Day weekend, according to the New York Times, bringing attention to a town that rarely attracts that sort of gathering.The proposed development remains a work in progress, though. Restoring historic structures in an isolated community is one challenge; creating the infrastructure needed for visitors and new residents is another.His wealth came from manufacturing, not propertyPoindexter's fortune was built long before Shafter became his major preservation project. He served in Vietnam, where he received two Silver Stars and two Purple Hearts, before spending 14 years working in finance. In 1985, he founded JB Poindexter & Co., a manufacturing group that he still owns.The company expanded through acquisitions and became a major supplier to the trucking industry. Its businesses manufacture truck bodies, including the brown delivery vehicles used by UPS. According to a 2024 EY announcement, the company had grown from $40 million in revenue in 1994 to more than $2.7 billion in annualised revenue.The company has also said it produces 66% of the step vans in the US class 5 delivery market. Poindexter's precise net worth is not publicly disclosed, but the New York Times describes him as a billionaire.Why Shafter’s revival differs from California ForeverIn California, a group of Silicon Valley investors spent about $800 million acquiring farmland in Solano County for California Forever, a proposed new city. That project sought to create something largely from the ground up and faced resistance from some local residents. There is already a town, even if only a small number of people remain. Its buildings, mine and history provide the foundation for the project. Instead of clearing land for a new settlement, Poindexter is attempting to reconstruct an older one and give it an economic purpose again.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: USS Lincoln nearly home after more than 300 days at sea
articles.summary: After spending more than 300 days at sea, service members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln will finally return home this week.
articles.body: After spending more than 300 days at sea, service members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln will finally return home this week. The beleaguered aircraft carrier with about 7,500 personnel is scheduled to dock Thursday in San Diego, amid sharp criticism over its prolonged deployment in the Middle East. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth acknowledged to crewmembers on Wednesday that he was the “only thing standing between you and home” and that he had been the one “who signed that orders book twice” to extend the ship’s deployment, The Associated Press reported. The Lincoln left San Diego in November and was initially expected to return before the summer months. Its deployment was extended after the Iran war began in February. The ship was at sea without a port of call for 286 days until early September, when it docked in Thailand for a handful of days. By that point, family members of those on board had raised concerns about dwindling food supplies and low morale. At least eight service members attempted suicide during the many months at sea, according to a letter sent last month to Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., by a top Navy official. The letter, obtained by NBC News, prompted concerns about the impact to mental health that such a lengthy deployment can have on service members. No deaths on the ship have been attributed to suicide. Some family members of those on the ship said the extended time at sea was “wreaking havoc” on sailors’ mental health, and one described it as a “scene out of the ‘American Horror Story’” television show. “Where he had been very positive, he started getting very dark,” one woman told NBC News about her son’s time at sea. Another parent said that she and her daughter, who is serving aboard the ship, grew increasingly frustrated as the Trump administration continued to push back the ship’s arrival date. According to U.S. officials, a sailor assigned to the air wing on the Lincoln went overboard in early August and was quickly rescued and treated. That sailor was transferred off the ship for further medical care, the official told NBC News. Navy officials initially said leadership had not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship. According to the letter, suicide attempts occurred among crewmembers and sailors from the carrier air wing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons.
